The Red worm lizard, Amphisbaena alba, is a fossorial squamate found throughout much of South America. Growth trajectories in this species are typically slow, with individuals eventually attaining a maximum total length of 75 cm [Li = 75 cm], a size that distinguishes it from smaller congerners within the Amphisbaenidae. Field studies focusing on reproductive maturation indicate that females reach puberty at a total length of 45.7 cm [Lp = 45.7 cm], while males mature slightly earlier at 42.2 cm [Lp = 42.2 cm], a difference that may reflect divergent energetic demands between the sexes. These size thresholds are critical for understanding population dynamics, as they mark the transition to reproductive viability. The ultimate length is achieved only after several years of steady growth, a pattern typical of species that invest heavily in skeletal and muscular tissue for burrowing.

When maintained at a stable incubation temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], hatchlings emerge from their leathery-shelled eggs after an incubation period of approximately 4.5 months, or roughly 137 days [ab = roughly 137 days]. The age at birth is thus closely tied to thermal environment, with cooler temperatures likely prolonging embryonic development. Upon emergence, neonates exhibit a wet body mass of 4.51 grams [Wwb = 4.51 grams], a modest initial weight that reflects the limited yolk reserves allocated to each offspring. This neonatal mass is comparable to values reported for Amphisbaena mertensi, where AndreNasc2006 documented a similar birth weight. The combination of protracted incubation and altricial-like hatchling size suggests a conservative reproductive strategy emphasizing offspring quality over quantity.

The annual clutch size is thus inferred from a small number of field-captured individuals, with considerable variation likely depending on maternal body condition and local prey availability. Further studies are needed to clarify whether multiple clutches can be produced in particularly favorable seasons, which would elevate the effective annual reproductive output.

Morphometric relationships in adults provide further insight into body condition and resource allocation. Specimens measuring 47 cm in snout-vent length typically have a short tail of approximately 3 cm and a corresponding wet body weight of 166.5 grams . This mass-length relationship offers a useful metric for assessing individual nutritional status, as deviations from the expected weight may indicate periods of food scarcity or reproductive burden. The relatively robust body mass for the length underscores the muscular, cylindrical morphology adapted for forceful burrowing in compact soils. Ecological comparisons with other fossorial reptiles suggest that the ratio of tail length to total body length in this species is unusually low, reflecting the reduced role of the tail in locomotion and fat storage.
